prime.problem: An agent says "Done, all tests pass" and its process exits cleanly. If you treat that as one fact, you ship failed work: the sentence, the exit status and the state of the repo come from different parts of the system and can disagree.
prime.fits: The third card of the runs course. Owning the session asked who owns a run and Retry, replay, resume asked who owns its progress; this card asks who owns the evidence that the run actually worked.
expect: a different owner and witness per link
prime.goal: Take any agent run, split its "done" into five links, name the evidence and owner for each, and say which link broke.

attend: In the Hermes cron run, which owner said "completed", and why was it not lying about what it owns?
Why can OpenCode's shell tool "complete" while the command it ran failed?
Both OpenCode runs printed the same sentence: which single piece of evidence tells them apart?
Where in the Tuesday run did "failed" first become "passing", and which link did that hide?
Why must the verifier sit outside the agent rather than read the agent's own test output?

must: Each link is recorded by a different owner (runtime, tool layer, process, verifier, channel) → each owner only reports its own lifecycle → a later link can be false while every earlier one is true → "done" must be decided per link, not from the last message

The final message is written by the model at the end of the loop → it is evidence only that the request completed → identical sentences can sit on top of a changed file and an unchanged one (OpenCode) → define done against the artifact you will accept

A tool returns a nonzero exit code as data, not as an error → "tool completed" stays true while "command succeeded" is false → a harness that checks only tool status, or a summary that drops the exit code, upgrades failure to success (status inflation)

The agent can misread, mis-summarize or edit its own evidence → effect verification has to be done by an owner outside the loop, on the final files, with unchanged tests → otherwise link 4 is just another claim
elevated: A scheduler ledger records the attempt, not the operation → Hermes cron said "completed" while both commands exited 2 and no receipt existed → scheduled work needs its own operation-level verifier and receipt, because nobody is watching when it runs
reference: OpenCode's six-link spelling of the chain (workspace changed, acceptance checks passed, patch accepted)
Hermes's list of separate records: operation, attempt, execution, verification, delivery
the versions tested: Hermes v0.20.6, OpenCode v1.18.30
the 91-byte Hermes fixture and the four execution contracts
the check() function's exact signature and regex

compress.prompt: Card closed: draw the five links as a row of boxes. Under each write its evidence and its owner, then colour the Tuesday run's links green or red and mark where the false claim entered.
checklist: request completed → tool completed → command succeeded → effect verified → delivered
evidence: final message · tool record · exit code · independent re-check of the artifact · delivery record
owners: runtime · tool layer · execution surface · outside verifier · control plane or channel
the false claim entered at the step-7 compaction summary (status inflation) and was repeated at step 9

retrieve.q: Explain what a false success claim is, using the two OpenCode runs, and say which link of the chain separates them.
answer: the final message asserts success but the world state disagrees
both runs said "The whitespace bug is fixed and the tests pass" and both CLIs exited successfully
only the tool-loop run changed the file and passed the unchanged tests: link 4, effect verified

retrieve.q: Walk through the Hermes cron negative control link by link: what each owner recorded, and why the ledger's "completed" was not a bug in the ledger.
answer: prompt punctuation was copied into both command arguments
both commands exited 2 (command succeeded ✗)
no operation receipt was written (effect verified ✗)
the ledger recorded the scheduler's attempt as completed, which is true of the attempt
the fix is a separate operation-level verifier, not a smarter ledger

retrieve.q: Re-running the full test suite after every agent run costs time. When would you skip independent verification, and what do you risk?
answer: skip it when there is no side effect (a chat answer, a read-only lookup)
keep it when the agent changes files, records or deployments, or runs unattended
skipping means trusting links 1–3 as a stand-in for link 4: exactly the gap both field cases show
a cheaper middle ground: check the diff exists and the tests are unchanged, re-run only the targeted tests

retrieve.q: Your checker gets ("All tests pass", 0, False). Which verdicts come out, and what probably happened in the run?
answer: request, tool and command all yes; effect verified NO; false success claim YES
the tests passed but nothing changed, so either the bug wasn't real in this workspace, the agent edited a different directory, or the tests don't cover the bug
the exit code alone can't tell these apart; inspect the diff and the working directory

compare.q: Agent evals grade the outcome with hidden tests; this card verifies one run's links. What is fundamentally the same, what differs in scale and purpose, and how does each fail?
answer: same: both trust the final state of the artifact, checked from outside, over the agent's claim
evals score many tasks × trials to estimate a pass rate; the claim chain decides whether one run's "done" is true
evals fail with visible or weak tests and too few tasks; the chain fails when the verifier is in-band or its scope is too narrow (three tests)
the false claim rate is what you get by running the chain check across an eval set

compare.q: Retry and resume make a run survive a crash. Why doesn't a successful resume prove the work was done, and which link does a durable runtime own?
answer: a durable runtime owns progress: which step ran, what to replay
a completed workflow is link 1 (and maybe 2), the same as the Hermes ledger's "completed"
after a crash mid-side-effect, the runtime may not know whether the effect happened; only an effect check settles it
so durable execution and the claim chain answer different questions: did it finish vs did it work

predict.q: You add a rule to the harness: the agent may only say "done" if its last pytest call exited 0. Which false claims does that stop, and name one it still lets through.
predict.answer: It stops the Tuesday-run kind, where the last test exit was nonzero. It does not stop a run that edits or deletes the failing test and then gets exit 0, a run that tested in the wrong working directory (like Hermes's goal run watching the wrong state), or a run whose tests don't cover the bug. All three keep link 3 green with link 4 false, because the rule is still checked by the agent's own evidence, not by an outside verifier on the files you'll accept.

apply.task: Run python3 code/done-chain.py, then add a fourth case for the Hermes cron negative run: ("completed", 2, False). Predict the six verdicts before running. Then extend check() with a fourth input, tests_unchanged, so a run that edits the test file can never be verified.
apply.done: The cron case prints request yes, tool yes, command NO, effect NO, delivered yes and false success claim no; you can say why the claim flag misses it and whether it should. And a call with exit 0, a non-empty diff and tests_unchanged=False prints effect verified NO.
apply.hint: "completed" doesn't match the CLAIM regex (done, fixed, tests pass, passing). A scheduler's status word is a success claim made by a different owner: decide whether to widen the regex or pass status words in as their own input.
